title: Velocity of a Quantum Particle in a Classically Forbidden Region
authors: Christian Beck, Sheldon Goldstein, Dustin Lazarovici, Roderich Tumulka, Nino Zanghi
abstract: Recently, Sharoglazova et al. [Nature 643, 67 (2025)] proposed a procedure for determining the speed of a quantum particle in the classically forbidden region of a potential step, and implemented it in a beautiful experiment. The inferred speeds disagree significantly with the Bohmian velocities, which the authors presented as an experimental challenge to Bohmian mechanics. This is puzzling because the speeds are inferred from particle populations in coupled waveguides for which Bohmian mechanics and standard quantum mechanics make identical predictions. We resolve the puzzle by a detailed theoretical analysis of the experimental setup. We show that the speed inference rests on an assumption that fails in the relevant (evanescent) regime according to both Bohmian mechanics and standard quantum mechanics -- namely that the inter-waveguide tunneling time is set by the transverse coupling and is not affected by entanglement with the longitudinal degree of freedom. We also consider a second speed estimate suggested by Sharoglazova et al., which is based on the Büttiker dwell time formula for particles in the forbidden region. We show that the authors applied the formula incorrectly, and that a correct application yields exact agreement with the predictions of Bohmian mechanics. Our analysis includes explicit calculations of Bohmian trajectories, dwell times, and longitudinal speeds in the two-dimensional waveguide model of the experiment.
summary: This theoretical work resolves a conflict regarding the measured speed of a quantum particle tunneling through a barrier, where experimental estimates disagreed with Bohmian predictions. The authors show that naive time estimates fail because they ignore entanglement between degrees of freedom. By correctly applying and conditioning the dwell-time formula, they demonstrate perfect agreement with Bohmian mechanics.
main_problem: The paper resolves discrepancies between particle speed estimates in classically forbidden regions (tunneling) derived from experiments/heuristics and predictions made by Bohmian mechanics.
main_result: A correct application of the dwell time formula, conditioned on penetration into the barrier, yields results that exactly agree with Bohmian mechanical predictions for the average velocity.
method: The analysis compares three methods—tunneling time estimate, Büttiker dwell time formula, and Bohmian trajectory calculation—by analyzing time-dependent wave packets in 1D and 2D coupled waveguide models.
model_or_system: The system is a non-relativistic quantum particle modeled by the Schrödinger equation in a potential landscape featuring a potential step realized via coupled waveguides (a double-well structure). The analysis covers both propagating and evanescent regimes.
key_observables: Particle populations ($|\Psi|^2$), Bohmian velocities, average speeds ($ ar{v}_B$), and conditional dwell times ($	au_{pen}$).
important_parameters: Evanescent decay constants ($\delta_\kappa,  ar{\kappa}$), energy splitting ($J_0$), spectral width ($\sigma_k$), and characteristic equilibration length scales ($X_{eq}$).
main_assumptions: The initial discrepancy arose from assuming the tunneling time is set only by transverse coupling (ignoring longitudinal entanglement) or applying the standard Büttiker formula without conditioning on barrier penetration.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate potential landscapes, relative population dynamics in both oscillatory (propagative) and monotonic (evanescent) regimes, and numerical simulations comparing $|\Psi|^2$ density with Bohmian trajectories.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the experimental challenge, then analyzing the theoretical estimates (tunneling time/dwell time), demonstrating where these estimates fail due to entanglement effects in the evanescent regime, and finally resolving the conflict by applying a corrected, conditional dwell-time argument that matches Bohmian predictions.
why_interesting: It provides deep insight into the interpretation of quantum measurements in non-trivial regimes (like tunneling) and rigorously tests the equivalence between different formalisms (QM vs. Bohmian mechanics) under specific physical constraints.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of the potential landscape underlying the experimental setup (dark: low, light: high). The main waveguide at y = y0 extends throughout; for x ≥0 the transverse potential becomes a double-well, side- coupling the main waveguide to a parallel auxiliary waveguide at y = −y0. At x = 0, there is a potential step, acting as a barrier for the particle incident from the main waveguide. An explicit form is given in (2) below.
Figure 2: Potentials V< and V> as in (2)

Figure 3: Relative population ρa in the auxiliary waveguide as a function of longitudinal distance from the step in units of |δk|−1. In the propagative regime (blue curve), the populations oscillate between the two waveguides, with complete transfer (ρa = 1) at odd multiples of π/(2δk). In the evanes- cent regime (orange curve, as given by (29)), the populations equilibrate monotonically, approaching ρa = 1/2 over the characteristic length scale Xeq ∼1/δκ.

Figure 4: Numerical simulation of Bohmian trajectories in the classi- cally forbidden region (x > 0) of the 2D setup for V0 = 0.54 meV, ℏJ0 = 26.2 µeV, Ek0 −V0 = −0.07 meV, σk = 2.5 × 10−3 µm−1. (a) Spatial paths of 5,000 trajectories sampled from |Ψ|2. Main waveguide centered around y0 = 10 µm; auxiliary waveguide centered around −y0 = −10 µm. (b) Longitudinal coordinate X(t) for 500 representative trajectories, exhibiting parabolic turnaround. Horizontal axis centered around median reversal time. (c) Transverse coordinate Y (t) for 292 trajectories that crossed y = 0 prior to turnaround; the simultaneous reversal of X(t) and Y (t) reflects the time- reversal symmetry (66).

Figure 5: Distribution of tunneling times for Bohmian trajectories migrating from the main into the auxiliary waveguide of the 2D setup. Here, “tunneling time” is defined as the time the Bohmian particle takes from entering the classically forbidden region at x = 0 (in the main waveguide, y > 0) until entering the auxiliary waveguide, y < 0. Top: Propagative regime (Ek0 − V0 = +0.15 meV). Bottom: Evanescent regime (Ek0 −V0 = −0.07 meV). σk = 2.5×10−3 µm−1 for both. Time is shown in units of π/(2J0). The orange curve shows for comparison the distribution of the first time of crossing from y > 0 to y < 0, p(τ) ≈(π/2) sin(πτ), in the 1D double well model (8) with initial state ϕm.
